# Bahudhātuka Sutta (MN 115 (PTS MN iii 61))
**ID:** MN 115 (PTS MN iii 61)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Bahudhātuka Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Many Elements
**PTS:** MN iii 61
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn115
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Bahudhātuka Sutta* ("Many Elements" or "The Many Kinds of Elements") is the 115th discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Segall 2003]. At the close of the discourse, the Buddha gives Ānanda several alternative titles for the text: *Catuparivatta* ("Four Chapters"), *Dhammādāsa* ("Mirror of the Dharma"), *Amatadundhubhi* ("Drum of the Deathless"), and *Anuttara Saṁgāmavijaya* ("Unsurpassed Victory in Battle") [Berkwitz 2006]. Spoken to Ānanda, the sutta takes wisdom as its primary theme, contrasting a wise person with a fool, whom it compares to a small fire capable of burning down an entire village [Anālayo 2014; Karma Sonam Palmo 2011]. According to the discourse, wisdom is cultivated by acquiring skill in four areas: the elements (*dhātu*), the sense fields (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), and what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna*) [SuttaCentral; Segall 2003].
While the Theravāda version in MN 115 enumerates forty-one elements, parallel traditions provide expanded classifications: an individual Chinese translation lists fifty-six elements, and Sarvāstivāda and Mūlasarvāstivāda texts enumerate sixty-two elements, as preserved in the *Madhyama-āgama*, the *Saṅgītiparyāya*, and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* [Anālayo 2014]. In the section on possibility and impossibility, the Pali sutta includes a doctrine of five gender-based impossibilities for women, declaring that a woman cannot become a wheel-turning monarch, a Buddha, or hold the positions of Brahmā, Śakra, or Māra [Anālayo 2017; Bodhi 2012]. Because this passage is absent from the Sarvāstivāda *Madhyama-āgama* parallel (MĀ 181), comparative scholars consider it to be a later accretion to the Theravāda discourse [Anālayo 2017; Bodhi 2012; Karma Sonam Palmo 2011].
Parallels to the text are found across Buddhist traditions: MĀ 181 and T 776 in Chinese, the *Dhātubahuka-sūtra* (D 297) in Tibetan translation, and complete discourse quotations in the Chinese *Dharmaskandha* (T 1537) and Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośoṭīkopāyikā* (D 4094) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2014; Karma Sonam Palmo 2011]. The discourse is widely cited across early canonical and para-canonical works, including the *Puggalapaññatti*, *Nettippakaraṇa*, *Kathāvatthu*, and *Milindapañha* [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus demonstrates substantial text reuse within the Pali canon, notably with the Abhidhamma's *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* (Vb 16) and *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga* (Vb 6), as well as the *Ekakanipāta* of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (AN 1.268–277) and the *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12) [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages of the sutta with the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra* and Vinaya texts such as the *Saṅghabhedavastu* [DharmaNexus].
